fetched_contents.text: Association between the APOE ε4 Allele and Late-Onset Alzheimer's Disease in an Ecuadorian Mestizo Population Abstract Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disease. It has two main pathological hallmarks: amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. The APOE ε4 allele has been recognized as the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) in several populations worldwide, yet the risk varies by region and ethnicity. The aims of this study were to describe APOE allele and genotype frequencies and examine the relationship between the APOE ε4 allele and LOAD risk in an Ecuadorian Mestizo population. We carried out a case-control study comprising 56 individuals clinically diagnosed with probable AD (≥65 years of age) and 58 unrelated healthy control subjects (≥65 years of age). Genotyping was performed using the real-time PCR method. Our data showed that allelic and genotypic frequencies follow the trends observed in most worldwide populations. We also found a high-risk association between APOE ε4 allele carriers and LOAD (OR = 7.286; 95% CI = 2.824–18.799; p < 0.001). Therefore, we concluded that APOE ε4 must be considered an important genetic risk factor for LOAD in the Ecuadorian Mestizo population. Additionally, we suggest that in mixed populations the effects of admixture and ethnic identity should be differentiated when evaluating genetic contributions to Alzheimer's disease risk. 1. Introduction Alzheimer's disease (AD) has emerged as the most prevalent form of late-life mental failure in humans, accounting for about 60–80% of dementia cases [1]. Alzheimer's Disease International (ADI) estimated that 46.8 million people worldwide were living with dementia in 2015 and predicted that this figure would reach 131.5 million in 2050 [2]. In Latin America, due to demographic and health transitions as well as low socioeconomic levels, it is expected that the number of people with dementia will rise from 7.8 million in 2013 to over 27 million by 2050 [3, 4]. The analysis of eight population studies conducted in Brazil, Cuba, Chile, Peru, and Venezuela showed that the global prevalence of dementia in Latin America has reached 7.1%, with AD being the most frequent type [5]. In Ecuador, there are no official data of prevalence or incidence of dementia. AD is a progressive and irreversible neurodegenerative disorder characterized by a decline in memory, language, problem-solving, and other cognitive skills that affect an individual's ability to perform daily activities [1]. The key neuropathological features of AD are extracellular plaques composed of β-amyloid peptides (Aβ) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), consisting of hyperphosphorylated tau proteins [6, 7]. Other neuropathological changes are synapse and neuronal loss, cerebral atrophy, gliosis, white matter degeneration, granulovacuolar degeneration, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), and other protein aggregates (TAR DNA-binding protein 43-immunoreactive inclusions, Lewy bodies, and actin-immunoreactive Hirano bodies) [7]. Based on the age of onset, AD is classified into two types: early-onset AD (EOAD, onset < 65 years of age) accounting for 1–5% of all cases and late-onset AD (LOAD, onset ≥ 65 years of age) accounting for >95% of them [8]. Three dominant inherited mutations in the genes amyloid precursor protein (APP), presenilin-1 (PS1), and presenilin-2 (PS2), which increase the production of amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides, have been linked to EOAD [9, 10]. Conversely, LOAD has been identified to be more complex involving multiple susceptibility genes and environmental factors [11]. Genetically, the APOE ε4 allele has been recognized as the strongest risk factor for LOAD [12–14]. Apolipoprotein E (APOE) is a glycoprotein of 299 amino acids with an estimated molecular mass of ~34 kDa that is involved in cholesterol transport and encoded by the APOE gene located in the long arm of the chromosome 19q13.2 [15]. The human APOE gene exists as three polymorphic alleles—ε2, ε3, and ε4—which differ by cysteine and arginine amino acids at residues 112 and 158, with ε2 (cys112, cys158), ε3 (cys112, arg158), and ε4 (arg112, arg158) [16]. The APOE ε4 allele has been related to earlier onset as well as higher risk for AD, and individuals with two copies of the APOE ε4 allele have a higher risk and earlier onset than heterozygous subjects [17]. Several studies have suggested mechanisms that could explain APOE ε4 allele's contribution to the pathogenesis of AD. These include the modulation of the deposition and clearance of Aβ, formation of plaques, impairment of the antioxidative defense system, dysregulation of the neuronal signaling pathways, disruption of cytoskeletal structure and function, and increased phosphorylation of tau with formation of neurofibrillary tangles [18]. Few APOE studies have been conducted in Latin America, and in Ecuador only two previous studies have investigated that gene. The first study evaluated frequencies of APOE genotypes and alleles in a population of Cayapas from Esmeraldas (n = 96) [19]. However, even though Cayapa Indians are part of the indigenous population living in Ecuador, Mestizos are the most numerous ethnic group accounting for approximately 60% of the total population. Ecuadorian Mestizos can be considered a trihybrid population resulting from the admixture of Amerindian, European, and African populations, having estimated average proportions of ~73, ~19, and ~8% in autosomal cells, respectively [20]. The second study evaluated the association between APOE ε4 and AD in a sample consisting of healthy (n = 39) and affected (n = 39) individuals from different provinces of Ecuador. Nevertheless, the ethnic composition was not detailed and no significant association was found in that study probably due to the limited sample size [21]. Biostatistics, School of Medicine, University of Mississippi Medical Center, Jackson, MS, United States * See more Article metrics View details Abstract Objective: To investigate whether APOE ε4 genotype—an established risk factor for dementia—is associated with earlier age at diagnosis in addition to increased risk overall and in secondary analysis by race and sex. Methods: We followed up 13,782 dementia-free individuals (n = 10,137 White, n = 3,645 Black, baseline age 60–66 years) in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study for up to 30 years. Dementia was operationalized using standardized algorithms incorporating longitudinal cognitive change, proxy report, and hospital or death certificate dementia codes. We used a mixture of generalized gamma distributions to simultaneously estimate time to dementia, time to dementia-free death, and the proportion of individuals with dementia, by APOE ε4 status (≥1 vs. no alleles). Results: Median age of dementia onset among APOE ε4 carriers was 81.7 (Blacks) and 83.3 years (Whites) compared with 82.6 (Blacks) and 85.7 years (Whites) in non-APOE ε4 carriers (p > 0.05 Blacks; p < 0.01 Whites). Age of dementia diagnosis did not differ by sex in ε4 carriers, but among non-carriers, average age was earlier in males than females regardless of race. APOE ε4 carriers had on average a higher proportion of diagnoses; results did not differ by race or sex. Conclusions:APOE ε4 carrier status is associated with earlier age of dementia diagnosis with differences across race and sex. These findings clarify the causal role of APOE in dementia etiology, which could help better identify at-risk subgroups and may help facilitate better research trial recruitment and design. Introduction Carriers of the apolipoprotein (APOE) ε4 allele contribute to 7% of incident global dementia cases and have double the risk of developing mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia (1, 2) than have non-carriers. Risk conferred by APOE ε4 varies by race and sex (3–6). However, most prior studies have been conducted in clinical, rather than population-based, samples. Although risk of dementia is greater in Blacks compared with Whites, the relative effect of APOE ε4 may be greater in Whites compared with Blacks, potentially because a larger component of the risk seen in Blacks is due to other health factors such as vascular disease (7–9). Additionally, most prior studies of APOE ε4 and dementia only estimate risk of dementia. By contrast, time to dementia by age (10, 11) allows for expansion upon current knowledge of the appropriate design and timing of dementia trials and may improve identification of people at risk for dementia at more appropriate ages. Human apolipoprotein E (ApoE) is a lipid transport protein coded by the polymorphic APOE gene, with three major alleles: ε2, ε3 and ε4. After age, the ε4 allele is the greatest risk factor for developing sporadic AD, conferring an increased risk of 3–4 and 8–12 times for one or two copies of the allele, respectively. This risk is reported to vary by demographic factors including sex, ethnicity and geography. In order to understand the risk of ApoE ε4 in relation to age, the primary risk factor for developing AD, we need to understand how the prevalence of APOE genotypes changes with age. Here, we present the first data on age-related prevalence of APOE ε4 in AD in three AD cohorts in Australia and the USA. There is a significant association between age and ε4 prevalence, particularly for ε4 homozygotes, such that as age increases the prevalence of ε4 decreases. Further studies on a random, population-based sample of the population are needed to provide more generalizable data, particularly in the >90-year-old age group. Early-stage AD symptoms include short-term memory loss, disorientation and language and behavioural problems, with an average life expectancy of less than 10 years following diagnosis (Liu et al. 2013; Todd et al. 2013). The number of people living with dementia globally is expected to rise to 65.7 million by 2030, and the burden is borne disproportionally by females and persons living in low-and middle-income countries (Prince et al. 2013). Human apolipoprotein E (ApoE) is a ~34-kDa, 299-aminoacid polypeptide, coded by the polymorphic APOE gene, mapped to chromosome 19q13.2. There are three major alleles designated ε2, ε3 and ε4, (Das et al. 1985) that encode three isoforms arising from a single cysteine-to-arginine amino acid substitution at positions 112 and 158 (positions 130 and 176, including the signalling peptide), producing ApoE2 (Cys112/ Cys158), ApoE3 (Cys112/Arg158) and ApoE4 (Arg112/ Arg158) (OMIM 2016). ApoE ε4 is recognised as the major single genetic risk factor for developing sporadic forms of AD (Corder et al. 1993). There is much evidence that APOE ε4 moves forward the age of onset of AD (Sweet et al. 2012) and also the rate of cognitive decline in preclinical AD (Pietrzak et al. 2015; Lim et al. 2016). Population context, penetrance, and modifiers

The evidence shows that APOE ε4 prevalence and effect size are not uniform across populations. In the population-level context provided, the ε4 allele frequency is reported as 14% globally, with much higher prevalence in some cohorts: 37% in Caucasians, 32% in African Americans, 19% in Hispanics, and 28% in Japanese [N4-F3]. This indicates that prevalence differs substantially by ethnicity and cohort, which is important because the same allele frequency can yield very different absolute numbers of carriers in different populations. The same source also notes that ε4 prevalence decreases with age, especially among homozygotes, and that this age-related pattern differs by demographic factors such as sex and ethnicity [N4-F3].

On penetrance and age of onset overlap, the evidence is mixed but clear in direction. APOE ε4 is described as the major single genetic risk factor for developing sporadic AD, with carriers having an increased risk of 3–4 times for one copy and 8–12 times for two copies [N4-F3]. The same source emphasizes that not all ε4 homozygotes develop AD: up to 50% of ε4/ε4 carriers in a first-degree relatives study survived to age 80 without disease [N4-F3]. This is a strong indication that penetrance and age of onset overlap in real cohorts, meaning that APOE4 increases risk but does not guarantee disease, and that the timing of disease onset can vary substantially among carriers.

The modifiers evidence points to several factors that change the APOE4 effect size. First, the evidence repeatedly notes that risk varies by demographic factors including sex, ethnicity, and geography [N4-F3]. Second, it identifies APOE2 as protective and APOE3 as neutral, which implies that the magnitude of APOE4 effects is modified by the presence of other alleles in the same locus [N5-R5]. Third, the evidence suggests that modifying factors such as APOB and sex can alter the effect, with APOE4 being a stronger risk factor for both men and women but with a different magnitude of effect by gender [N5-R2]. This means that APOE4 is not a fixed effect across all cohorts; its size depends on background genetics and other host factors.

Overall, the population context is best summarized as: APOE ε4 prevalence varies widely by ethnicity and cohort; carriers face increased risk but not guaranteed disease; and the effect size is modified by sex, ethnicity, APOE2/APOE3 background, and other factors [N4-F3][N5-R2][N5-R5].
node_outputs.N10:
Determine how apoE4 copy number shifts the age of onset distribution

The evidence is consistent in one direction but heterogeneous in magnitude and definitions. The strongest statement is that APOE ε4 is associated with earlier age of dementia diagnosis compared to non-carriers, and this effect differs by race and sex [N2-F2]. In the ARIC cohort, median age of dementia onset was 81.7 years among Black APOE ε4 carriers and 83.3 years among White carriers, versus 82.6 and 85.7 years among non-carriers, respectively [N2-F2]. The source also notes that age of dementia diagnosis did not differ by sex in ε4 carriers, but non-carriers had earlier onset in males than females regardless of race [N2-F2]. These findings show that APOE4 copy number shifts the age of onset distribution earlier, but the effect is not uniform across subgroups.

Study-specific onset definitions and cutoffs are important because the evidence shows different operationalizations. The Frontiers study explicitly uses dementia diagnosis or dementia-free death as the outcome and models both age of diagnosis and risk of diagnosis within the same analysis [N2-F2]. The NIH and Alzheimer’s.gov summaries also use age-specific estimates, such as people carrying two APOE4 copies having a 60% chance of developing AD dementia by age 85 [N6-R1][N7-R2]. In another source, APOE4 double-carriers who developed AD symptoms did so around 65 years of age, which is 7–10 years earlier than non-carriers [N7-R4]. These cutoffs matter because they define what counts as “earlier onset” and can change the apparent magnitude of the effect.

How one copy differs from two copies is less directly quantified in the supplied evidence, but the pattern is clear. APOE ε4 carriers, regardless of whether they have one or two copies, are associated with earlier dementia diagnosis than non-carriers [N2-F2]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison of one versus two copies on onset age, so the distinction between heterozygosity and homozygosity is not fully resolved here. Instead, the evidence suggests that the overall effect of APOE4 is to shift the distribution earlier, with the strongest reported effect in homozygous carriers [N2-F2][N6-R1].

The evidence also shows that the onset effect varies by age group and gender. In the ARIC cohort, the earlier onset effect was present in both Black and White groups, but the magnitude differed between races, and age of diagnosis did not differ by sex in ε4 carriers, while non-carriers had earlier onset in males than females [N2-F2]. This indicates that the age-onset shift is not uniform across the entire population. The evidence also notes that APOE ε4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for LOAD and causes an earlier age of symptom onset compared to other factors [N6-R3]. Taken together, the evidence supports that APOE4 copy number moves the onset distribution earlier, but the exact timing depends on cohort definition, race, and sex [N2-F2][N6-R3].
node_outputs.N9:
Quantify the risk effect of one versus two apoE4 alleles

The evidence provides a consistent dose-response pattern, though the exact estimates vary by source and population. The strongest direct statement is that one copy of the ε4 allele increases risk 3–4 times, while two copies increase it 8–12 times [N4-F3]. Another source states that APOE4 homozygotes have a lifetime risk approaching 60% by age 85, consistent with a very strong dose-dependent effect [N8-R3]. A more recent source says that two copies “boost the odds up to 15-fold,” while the Mayo Clinic summary says one copy “doubles or triples” the risk [N4-R4][N3-R1]. These estimates overlap, but they are not identical, which suggests that the effect size depends on study design, population, and whether the risk is expressed as odds ratio, relative risk, or lifetime probability.

How risk varies by study design and population is evident in the supplied evidence. The Ecuadorian Mestizo study reports an odds ratio of 7.286 for APOE ε4 carriers compared with non-carriers, indicating a strong but population-specific effect [N1-F1]. The Frontiers study reports age-related prevalence of ε4, emphasizing that the effect diminishes after 70 years of age and that prevalence differs by sex and ethnicity [N4-F3]. The APOE2/APOE4 study notes that APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for LOAD while APOE2 is protective, suggesting that background alleles and population structure can change the observed effect size [N5-R5]. Taken together, the evidence supports a dose-dependent pattern, but the exact relative risk depends on the study’s population, age range, and how risk is measured.

Whether the effect is additive or multiplicative is not directly stated, but the evidence suggests a multiplicative or semidominant pattern. The APOE ε4 allele is described as conferring an increased risk of 3–4 times for one copy and 8–12 times for two copies [N4-F3], which is consistent with a multiplicative or semidominant model rather than a simple additive one. The same source also says that risk varies by demographic factors, implying that the relationship is not linear in all populations [N4-F3]. The evidence further supports a dose-dependent pattern: having one copy increases risk, and having two copies increases it further, with homozygosity associated with the highest risk [N4-F3][N8-R3].

Overall, the risk evidence is best summarized as: one copy increases risk 3–4 times, two copies increase it 8–12 times or more, the effect is dose-dependent, and the magnitude varies by study design, population, and background alleles such as APOE2 and APOE3 [N4-F3][N8-R3][N1-F1].
node_outputs.N12:
Separate heterozygous from homozygous carrier effects on risk and onset

The evidence supports distinct effects for heterozygotes and homozygotes, especially in terms of magnitude. For risk, the provided material states that one copy of the ε4 allele increases risk 3–4 times, while two copies increase it 8–12 times [N4-F3]. Another source notes that homozygous APOE4 carriers have the highest Aβ pathology burden and that APOE4 homozygotes have earlier onset of AD biomarker changes and clinical decline than heterozygotes or ε3/ε4 carriers [N8-R1][N8-R5]. This indicates that homozygosity changes the magnitude of the effect, making the risk and disease-related changes larger than in heterozygosity.

The evidence also suggests that heterozygous effects are often smaller or less consistent than homozygous effects. The Mayo Clinic summary says one copy “doubles or triples” the risk, which is a broad and less precise estimate than the more specific 3–4 times figure [N3-R1]. In contrast, the homozygous effect is described as 8–12 times increased risk and as approaching 60% lifetime risk by age 85 [N4-F3][N8-R3]. The heterozygous effect is also less consistent across studies because the supplied evidence includes both general statements and more specific cohort estimates [N3-R1][N4-F3]. This inconsistency is likely because heterozygosity is less extreme than homozygosity and therefore more sensitive to population structure and study design.

For onset timing, the evidence is again clearer for homozygotes. The APOE ε4 homozygotes have earlier onset of AD biomarker changes and clinical decline than heterozygotes or ε3/ε4 carriers [N8-R1]. The same source also notes that homozygous individuals face a lifetime risk approaching 60% by age 85 [N8-R3]. In contrast, the supplied evidence for heterozygous onset effects is less directly quantified, but it does show that APOE ε4 carriers in general have earlier dementia diagnosis than non-carriers [N2-F2]. That broader pattern suggests that heterozygous carriers also shift the onset distribution earlier than non-carriers, but the supplied evidence does not show a direct head-to-head comparison between heterozygotes and homozygotes on onset timing.

Taken together, the heterozygous versus homozygous distinction matters because homozygosity increases both risk magnitude and the speed of disease-related changes, while heterozygous effects are smaller and less consistent across studies [N4-F3][N8-R1][N8-R3].

## How carrying one or two copies of the APOE4 allele affects risk and age of onset of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease

The evidence consistently supports a dose-dependent effect of APOE4 copy number: **one copy increases risk, and two copies increase it further**, with the strongest observed effects for homozygosity [N4-F3][N8-R3]. Across the supplied sources, the most direct estimates are that one copy increases risk **3–4 times**, while two copies increase it **8–12 times** or **up to 15-fold**, depending on the source and how risk is expressed [N4-F3][N4-R4][N3-R1]. This pattern suggests that APOE4 contributes in a **multiplicative or semidominant** fashion rather than in a simple additive way [N4-F3][N8-R3].

### 1) Risk effect by copy number
